The resulting six-carbon compound is immediately broken down into two three-carbon compounds, 3-PGA [ev_007]. The energy in ATP and NADPH is then used to convert the three-carbon 3-PGA into G3P, a reduction reaction that involves the gain of electrons [ev_007] [ev_003]. Because CO2 is fixed from its inorganic form into organic molecules, this is called carbon fixation [ev_007]. Each turn makes two G3P molecules, and three turns fix enough net carbon to export one G3P, while the remaining G3P molecules are used to regenerate RuBP so the cycle can prepare for more CO2 to be fixed [ev_002]. One G3P leaves the cycle to contribute to the formation of a carbohydrate molecule, commonly glucose, which requires six turns of the cycle for six carbon atoms [ev_001]. The remaining G3P molecules stay in the cycle to be formed back into RuBP, which is ready to react with more CO2 [ev_003] [ev_001]. ATP is also used in the regeneration of RuBP [ev_001].
exact_original_fixed_initial_response.short_answer: RuBisCO combines CO2 with RuBP; the six-carbon product splits into two 3-PGA, which ATP and NADPH reduce to G3P [ev_007]. Most G3P is recycled to regenerate RuBP, while one G3P per three turns is exported for carbohydrate formation [ev_002] [ev_003].
